payload.title: Rooftops for Rent
paragraphs: Ten years ago, keeping bees on a city roof was a mild act of rebellion, practised by a few enthusiasts who carried their equipment up fire escapes. Today it is a service that can be ordered by email. Hotels, banks and museums lease hives by the year, photograph the harvest for their annual reports, and hand small jars of honey to visitors as proof that the building is doing something for nature.

Ecologists have watched this boom with growing unease, because the honeybee is a farm animal rather than a wild one. A single managed hive sends out tens of thousands of foragers, and in a dense district they strip the same limited flowers that solitary bees and hoverflies depend on. Surveys in London and Paris have found neighbourhoods where the density of hives now exceeds anything the surrounding gardens could plausibly feed. The pollinators genuinely at risk are the wild species, and they do not live in boxes.

None of this makes the rooftop keepers villains; it makes their enthusiasm badly aimed. What a city can offer that farmland cannot is scruffiness: road verges left unmown until midsummer, balconies planted with lavender rather than turf, dead wood tolerated in a corner of a park. Such measures photograph poorly and produce nothing to put in a jar, which is exactly why they need arguing for.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Urban beekeeping has grown into a corporate gesture that can actually harm the wild pollinators it is meant to help, and cities would do better to provide untidy, flower-rich habitat instead.
Honeybees are dying out in cities, so companies should be encouraged to lease many more rooftop hives than they currently do.
Rooftop beekeepers are dishonest people who know perfectly well that their hives damage wildlife and continue regardless.
Because wild bees cannot be counted accurately, ecologists have no reliable evidence about what is happening to pollinators in cities.

questions.before: The writer stresses that the honeybee is a farm animal in order to suggest that adding hives to a city no more helps wild insects than adding cattle to a field would

payload.title: The Second Life of Cloth
paragraphs: The bin outside the supermarket promises that your old clothes will be recycled, and most shoppers picture the jumper they dropped in becoming another jumper. Very little of it works that way. Sorters open the bags, pull out whatever can be resold as it is, and send the rest abroad or to a shredder, where it is torn into short fibres and pressed into insulation, mattress filling or industrial wipes.

The obstacle is chemistry rather than goodwill. A shirt described as cotton is usually cotton spun together with elastane, dyed, coated and finished with several substances that no label records. Separating those components costs more than growing new cotton, and shredding shortens the fibres so severely that they can rarely be spun into thread again. Recyclers therefore speak carefully of downcycling, a word that concedes the material is moving one step closer to the landfill each time.

Designers who take the problem seriously have concluded that recycling has to begin at the drawing board. A garment made from a single fibre, sewn with thread of the same material and fastened with buttons that can be cut off in one pass, can genuinely be turned back into cloth. Such garments are duller to design and slower to make, and they will only be made in quantity if buyers stop treating the recycling bin as an excuse.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Most collected clothing cannot become new clothing because of the way garments are blended and finished, so real textile recycling depends on designing simpler, single-fibre garments from the start.
Clothing collection bins are a deliberate fraud, and the companies that run them know that everything placed inside is sent straight to landfill.
Recycling cotton is technically straightforward, and the only reason it is not done more widely is that shoppers refuse to pay slightly higher prices.
Because synthetic fibres last far longer than natural ones, the textile industry should abandon cotton entirely in favour of elastane blends.
